title: Naam japo, deeper
hook: remembrance as the root of everything else

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirat karo: earn by honest work, and give from the hand. Your line was work as prayer. How did the hour you chose go? Was there one moment you did it more honestly than usual? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

The morning after a storm, two old trees on one street. One is down across a lawn, its whole underside lifted into the air, a flat plate of soil and short roots. The tree next to it, just as tall, is still standing, missing a few branches. From above the ground they looked the same. The difference was underneath, where nobody could see it. Yesterday was the branches: honest work, out in the world. Tomorrow will be the fruit: sharing. Today is the part underground. Of the three phrases, today's is the one this week sets at the root.
screen: `TWO TREES, ONE STORM.` → `THE DIFFERENCE IS UNDERNEATH.` → `TODAY: THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: Naam japo. Naam is the Name, the word Sikhs use for the presence of the One, not a label but something lived with. Japo means repeat it, remember it, keep it going. And Guru Nanak's own lines show why it sits underneath the rest. In the Japji, the morning prayer, he says, in paraphrase: in the ambrosial hours before dawn, reflect on the true Name and its greatness. That's amrit vela, the early hours some Sikhs keep for this. Remembrance comes first in the day, before the work. Then, in a hymn in Raga Asa that Sikhs sing in the evening prayer, there's a line short enough to carry: saying it, I live; forgetting it, I die. That's how strongly he puts it. The Name isn't an extra. It's breath. And one more picture from the Japji. When the hands and feet and body are covered in dirt, water washes them clean. When the mind is stained, it's washed by love of the Name. Put the three together and the shape is clear. Remembering comes before the day. Forgetting is like a kind of dying. And the mind gets clean the way hands do, by going back to the water again and again. That's why it's the root. Honest work done without it can turn hard. Sharing done without it can turn proud. With it underneath, the work and the sharing have something to stand on when the wind comes. You don't see a root. You only see what it holds up. That's today's line.
screen: `NAAM: THE NAME, LIVED WITH.` · `BEFORE DAWN, REFLECT ON THE NAME.` · `SAYING IT, I LIVE.` · `THE MIND WASHED LIKE HANDS.` · then, large: `THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember before working. In the sit, let the breath slow. Think of the next piece of work waiting for you, a task, a call, a sink full of dishes. Before you touch it, go underneath it. On each breath in, rest your attention on the One, however you understand that. If you pray, you can say Waheguru silently, once on the breath in, once on the breath out. If you don't, simply notice the breath as something given. Let the work wait for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Naam japo. Remember the Name and keep remembering it, the part of Guru Nanak's way that sits underneath work and sharing. Today's word.
Your line: the root. Before each new task today, take one breath of remembering first, then begin. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs practice naam japo through nitnem, the daily prayers, through simran, repeating Waheguru, and through kirtan; some rise in amrit vela, the hours before dawn, to begin the day with it.

match.prompt: the root, in Nanak's words: tap the pairs.
pairs: washed by love of the Name

myth: in the Japji, water washes the body, but the mind is washed by love of the Name
the Japji sets the two side by side: dirt on the hands, stain on the mind, and what cleans each.
in the Asa hymn, Nanak says forgetting the Name is a small thing
he puts it as strongly as he can: saying it, I live; forgetting it, I die.
the Japji places reflection on the Name in the hours before dawn
it speaks of the ambrosial hours, amrit vela, for reflecting on the true Name and its greatness.

fork.setup: you have three things to do today: work honestly, share, and remember the Name. which one does the lesson put underneath the other two?
fork.reveal: remembrance is the root: it comes before the day's work in the Japji, and the other two stand on it.

original.note: naam is the Name; japo means repeat it, remember it.

trapdoor: what you thought: naam japo means saying a word over and over.
what it means: living with the Name, remembering it underneath everything else in the day.
what a scholar hears: amrit vela in the Japji, and the Asa line saying it I live, forgetting it I die.
